Section 1 of 4

From molecule to medicine

How a chemical becomes a medicine you can buy.

Why it matters: every pill your future clients take went through this pipeline. Knowing its weak points tells you how far to trust "clinically proven".

Chapter 4 · p. 101 Updated

What changed after thalidomide?

Before 1962

New drugs were judged mainly by testimonials: enthusiastic reports from the doctors involved, with no proper comparison group.

The disaster

Thalidomide, taken for morning sickness early in pregnancy, caused serious limb deformities. Updated About 10,000 babies were affected worldwide.

The response

Countries set up or strengthened regulators: government bodies that decide whether a drug may be sold (UK: Committee on Safety of Drugs, 1963; US: the FDA, Food and Drug Administration). A 1962 US law made two things compulsory: proof that a drug works, and informed consent (patients agree after being told the risks).

Guess: thalidomide comes in two mirror-image forms, like a left and a right hand. Only one causes the harm. Would giving only the "safe" form have prevented it?

No. In the body the two forms turn into each other within hours, so the "safe" form soon becomes a mix. Lecture 3

Why it matters: the rules for testing every drug today were written in response to this tragedy.

Chapter 4 · pp. 101–102, 107 Updated Book correction

How many molecules does it take to make one medicine?

Guess first: out of 10,000 new chemicals (compounds) a company makes, how many become a medicine?

Leonard (2003)

Pre-clinical tests (lab and animals, before any person takes it): 5–7 years. Phases 1–3 (testing in people): at least 6 years. In total at least 12 years and over $230 million.

Updated Today

A typical new drug now costs about $985 million to develop, because the cost of all the failures is included.

Wouters et al., JAMA, 2020: 63 drugs approved 2009–2018

Book correction (p. 107): the book says "10 million" of 10,000 compounds enter Phase 1. That is a misprint: about 10 do.

Why it matters: almost everything fails, so companies have huge pressure to make the survivors look good.

Chapter 4 · p. 102 Not in the book Debate

Can a mouse be depressed?

Hands up: can a dog be depressed? A mouse?

Leonard (2003)

"Only man appears to suffer from any of the major psychiatric disorders." So animal models (animals given something like a human disorder, so drugs can be tested on them) can only copy some behaviours.

But the evidence is mixed

• Animals kept in poor conditions (mice in barren cages, chronically stressed rats, pigs) show depression-like signs: low activity, not responding, losing interest in pleasure.

• A 2021 review called this "troubling evidence", but found no case yet confirmed as depression in the full sense doctors diagnose in people.

• Vets treat behavioural disorders: fluoxetine (Prozac) was approved in the US in 2007 for separation anxiety in dogs (distress when left alone).

MacLellan, Fureix, Polanco & Mason, Behaviour, 2021: narrative review

The catch: we can't ask a mouse how it feels. Symptoms we only know from words (guilt, hopelessness, hearing voices) can't be checked.

Why it matters: if the animal's problem isn't quite the human illness, a drug that "works" in mice can fail in people.

Chapter 4 · pp. 102–103 Exam Book correction

How good is an animal model?

Validity = how well an animal model stands in for the human illness. There are three ways to judge it.

Kind of validityWhat it meansExample
PredictiveDoes the drug's effect in the animal predict its effect in patients?Antidepressants make rats keep swimming longer before giving up in a water tank (the "swim test")
FaceDo the animal's changes look like the patient's symptoms?Stressed mice lose interest in sugar water, like loss of pleasure in depression
ConstructAre the causes the same as in the human illness?Long-term unpredictable stress, a known trigger of human depression

Sort: click each to cycle predictive → face → construct.

Knock-out mice

One gene switched off, e.g. for a receptor (a docking site for a brain chemical). Over-expressing mice make extra of a protein, e.g. beta-amyloid, which clumps in Alzheimer's. Both show what a chemical does to behaviour.

Why it matters: no animal model has all three, so most models only test whether a new drug acts like the old ones.

Chapter 4 · pp. 101–104, 109–110 Updated

Planned or lucky? Where new drugs come from

Planned: start from human biology

Our genes are 98.9% the same as a chimpanzee's, but our brains switch them on over 5 times as much. So animals show how a drug is handled by the body, not easily disorders of the mind.

Test on human cells earlier: microarrays (chips that read thousands of genes at once), stem cells (cells that can grow into brain cells).

Aim at many targets, not one. A target is the protein a drug acts on, e.g. the serotonin transporter for SSRIs. The brain has back-up systems, so blocking just one can be worked around.

Lucky: most drug families found by chance

The first antidepressants (the tricyclics and MAO inhibitors, two older drug families) were discovered by accident, and so was mianserin.

Labs then screened for copies, giving "me-too" drugs (close copies of a successful drug), such as the SSRIs: fewer side effects, but no better at treating.

Most lab tests look at one dose, but patients take drugs for weeks.

Updated Drugs that work in a genuinely new way are rare. Two recent ones: esketamine nasal spray for depression (2019), and Cobenfy for schizophrenia (2024), the first in about 30 years that doesn't work by blocking dopamine.

Why it matters: a "new" drug is often a copy of an old one. Ask what is actually new about it.

Section 2 of 4

The clinical trial

A planned experiment in people that tests whether a treatment works and is safe.

Why it matters: "clinically proven" is printed on many packets. This section shows what it should mean.

Chapter 4 · pp. 104–105 Key study not in the book

How would you test Seravexa?

Your plan first: who gets it, compared with what, and how would you know it worked?

Bradford Hill's definition

A clinical trial is "a carefully, and ethically, designed experiment" that answers precisely framed questions, using equal groups, formed at random and treated at the same time.

Leonard: a trial should tell us

(a) does it work? (b) is it better than a standard drug (an existing drug known to work)? (c) who benefits? (d) best route, dose and how often? (e) what are the side effects?

Key study: streptomycin, 1948

The UK Medical Research Council tested streptomycin for tuberculosis, with patients allocated by random numbers in sealed envelopes. Designed by Bradford Hill, it is often called the first modern randomised controlled trial: patients split by chance into a treated group and a comparison ("control") group.

Optional extra. In 1747 James Lind gave 12 sailors with scurvy six different treatments; the pair given oranges and lemons recovered. A fair comparison, but not random.
Title page, 1757 edition. Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0

Chapter 4 · p. 105 Exam

Should the doctor choose who gets Seravexa?

40 people with depression volunteer. Half will get Seravexa, half a dummy pill (placebo). Each dot is one person: the darker the dot, the more depressed they are at the start.

How depressed each group is at the start (average depression score, 0–100). For a fair test, the two bars should be about equal.

Seravexa group
–
Placebo group
–

Who should get Seravexa? Try Way 1, then Way 2.

Three rules of a randomised trial

1. Groups formed by chance, so they match in age, sex, how ill they are, and things we haven't even measured.

2. Treated at the same time and place. Comparing with past patients ("historical controls") is almost always unacceptable.

3. The question fixed in advance, e.g. "Does Seravexa treat depression faster, better and with fewer side effects than drug B?"

Why it matters: letting chance decide (randomisation) removes systematic bias: a difference built into the groups that always pushes the result one way.

Chapter 4 · p. 106 Exam Updated

Who knows who got what?

Patient

Knows

Doctor scoring the patient

Knows

The list of who got which pill

Open to all

Everyone knows. Used for first tests in people (Phase 1): finding the dose range and side effects.

Patient

Doesn't know

Doctor scoring the patient

Knows

The list of who got which pill

Doctor has it

Identical-looking pills, so the patient can't tell. But the doctor knows, and their hopes can colour the scores.

Patient

Doesn't know

Doctor scoring the patient

Doesn't know

The list of who got which pill

Locked away

Neither the patient nor the doctor scoring them knows until the end. The standard for testing whether a drug works.

Why "blind"? Patients and doctors both expect things. Hope makes patients feel better, and makes doctors score them as better.

When blinding fails: a drug's side effects give it away (Leonard). Updated With psychedelics (drugs that change perception, e.g. psilocybin, MDMA) most patients can tell they got the drug; this was one concern when the FDA rejected MDMA-assisted therapy for PTSD (post-traumatic stress disorder) in August 2024.

Chapter 4 · pp. 107–108 Exam Updated

Why give anyone a dummy pill?

A placebo is a dummy pill: it looks exactly like the real one but contains no drug.

Guess: in depression, what % improve on a dummy pill? On an antidepressant?

30%Placebo
60%Antidepressant

Leonard, 2003: improvement, as a share of the best possible

Updated On average drugs beat placebo by 1.75 points on the Hamilton scale (a 0–52 depression score; higher = worse), but about 15% of patients get a large extra benefit.
Stone et al., BMJ, 2022. Graph: Kirsch et al., 2008, CC BY 2.5

So a placebo group…In everyday words
separates mind effectsAny pill from an enthusiastic doctor helps a bit (the "halo" effect).
separates the illness's ups and downsDepression often lifts by itself for a while.
rules out false negativesA false negative is wrongly concluding a drug doesn't work. With a standard drug in the trial too, we can tell a bad drug from a bad trial (slide 17).

Chapter 4 · p. 107 Exam

In a trial with three groups, what if all three improve the same?

Each group in a trial is called an arm. Here: placebo, Seravexa, and a standard drug (an existing drug already known to work). Bars show how much each group improved.

RESULT

Click a result, discuss what it means, then press "What does it mean?"

A trial that finds "no difference" may mean…

• too few patients to see a real effect

• the dose was too low

• the outcome measure (the scale used to score improvement) couldn't pick up the change

• the trial design couldn't tell an active drug from an inactive one

Why it matters: without a standard drug in the trial, a negative result can't tell you whether the drug failed or the trial did.

Chapter 4 · pp. 106–107 Exam Updated

What does each phase test?

Putting it together: stops 5–7 of Seravexa's journey, plus what happens after it goes on sale.

PhaseQuestionWho takes itDesign (Leonard)
Phase 1Is it safe? What dose range? Which side effects?Healthy volunteers first, then a small group of well-defined patientsOpen: everyone knows what they're taking
Phase 2Does it work, compared with a standard drug?PatientsDouble-blind (slide 14), against a standard drug
Phase 3Does it work and stay safe in a big, varied group?Large numbers of patientsDouble-blind, at many hospitals ("multicentre")
Phase 4What happens in everyday use? Any rare side effects?Everyone prescribed itNot in the book Monitoring after it goes on sale

Updated Today, Phase 2 is usually a smaller placebo-controlled trial to find early signs it works and the right dose. For some psychiatric drugs, Phase 1 is done in patients, because the side effects are too strong for healthy volunteers. In the exam, use Leonard's descriptions.

Why it matters: Phases 1–3 take at least 6 years, yet rare side effects may only appear in Phase 4.

Chapter 4 · pp. 107–108 Exam Local and updated

Is it fair to give a depressed patient a dummy pill, and could we run this trial safely in Pakistan?

Is it fair? Benefits versus harms of giving placebo

Could we run it safely here? Approval, consent, follow-up, cost

Leonard

A depressed patient left on placebo for weeks could harm themselves, so patients at high risk are usually excluded (not allowed to join). Yet every regulator insists on placebo-controlled trials.

Consent and crossover

Informed consent needs a check of mental state: able to communicate, with memory and orientation (knowing who and where they are) intact. Crossover: each patient takes drug and placebo in turn; watch for carry-over (the drug's effect lingering).

Here and now In Pakistan a trial needs approval from DRAP (Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan) and an ethics committee (a panel that checks the study protects the people in it). Worldwide: the Declaration of Helsinki, the code of ethics for research on people (revised 2024).

Why it matters: a trial can be scientifically perfect and still wrong if patients are harmed.

Section 3 of 4

Reading the numbers

How researchers decide whether a difference is real or just chance.

Why it matters: almost every psychology paper reports "p < 0.05". This section shows what it does, and doesn't, tell you.

Chapter 4 · p. 105 Exam Book correction

Is this coin biased?

–

Guess before each flip: how many heads would make you suspicious?

The null hypothesis

Start by assuming there is no difference: the coin is fair, or Seravexa does nothing. Then ask how surprising our result would be if that were true.

Statistically significant: p < 0.05

p is a probability: a difference this big would turn up by chance 5 or fewer times in 100 if the drug did nothing. So we doubt the "no difference" assumption.

Book correction (p. 105): "once in 100 trials" is P ≤ 0.01, not P ≤ 0.001 as printed.

Why it matters: "significant" means "probably not chance". It does not prove the drug works, or that the difference matters (slide 27).

Chapter 4 · pp. 105–106 Exam

How sure are we? Confidence intervals

Suppose 25% improve a lot on Seravexa and 10% on placebo: a true gain of 15 percentage points (25 − 10). Drag to change the trial size.

The 95% confidence interval

The bar on the chart: the range we're 95% sure the true effect lies in. Narrow = precise. Wide = we don't really know yet.

If the interval crosses zero, "no benefit" is still possible: the result is not significant. More patients make the interval narrower.

Leonard: small trials are often published with no statement of power (the chance a trial can detect a real effect, slide 25) and no confidence intervals, which would reveal how weak they are.

Chapter 4 · p. 106 Exam

Two ways to get it wrong

Really: Seravexa works
Really: Seravexa does nothing
Trial concludes: it works

Correct (True Positive)

A real effect, found.

Type 1 error (False Positive)

A difference that isn't real. A false alarm.

Court: convicting an innocent person.

Trial concludes: no difference

Type 2 error (False Negative)

Missing a difference that is real. Often because the trial was too small.

Court: letting a guilty person go.

Correct (True Negative)

No effect, none found.

A small trial says a new pill beats placebo; three big trials find no effect.
A study of 16 patients misses a drug that really works.
A smoke alarm goes off when nothing is burning.
A pregnancy test says "not pregnant" when she is.

Chapter 4 · pp. 106, 110 Exam Book update

Can a drug that works fail its trial?

Guess first: Seravexa really works. If 20 research teams each run a 30-patient trial, how many will find that it works?

HOW WELL IT REALLY WORKS

Respond on placebo: 30%

–

Green = the trial found a significant difference (p < 0.05). Red = it didn't.

Book update (p. 106): Leonard says a non-significant result means "no clinically useful difference". Today: absence of evidence is not evidence of absence.

1

With 30 patients (15 per group) and Leonard's effect, only about 1 trial in 4 finds it.

2

The rest miss a drug that works: a Type 2 error, from low statistical power (the chance of finding a real effect).

3

With 200 patients, about 99 in 100 trials find Leonard's effect.

4

With the modern effect (25% vs 10%), even 200 patients miss it 1 time in 4.

Exam-style question · 2.5 marks Write on your own · 5 minutes

Practise: write your answer

A newspaper headline says: "New anxiety pill doesn't work." The study gave the pill or a placebo to 16 adults with anxiety and found no statistically significant difference (p = 0.30).

Explain two reasons why this result does not show that the pill is ineffective. (2.5 marks)

What a full answer includes

  • Any two reasons, each named and explained (about 1.25 marks each):
  • Low statistical power: with only 8 per group, a real difference can easily be missed (a Type 2 error).
  • No standard drug in the trial: without a drug known to work, we can't tell whether the pill failed or the trial was unable to detect any effect.
  • Dose too low, or an outcome measure / trial length that couldn't pick up the change.
  • Strong answers add the fix: a larger trial planned with a power calculation.

Chapter 4 · p. 106 Exam Updated

Significant is not the same as important

Leonard's examples

Beta receptors (docking sites for adrenaline) on white blood cells change by over 50% between midday and midnight in healthy adults.

The serotonin transporter (the pump SSRIs block) on blood platelets is one-third more active at noon than at 6 a.m.

Both are real, measurable differences, and neither matters to health.

Updated Back to antidepressants

Stone et al. (2022): the average drug–placebo difference, 1.75 points on a 52-point depression scale, is highly significant because the trials were huge.

Is 1.75 points important to a patient? That is a separate question from "is it real?"

Statistical significance asks: is the difference probably real? Clinical significance asks: is it big enough to matter to patients? Always ask both.

Why it matters: with enough patients, almost any tiny difference becomes "significant".

Section 4 of 4

Trials together, and their limits

What we learn by combining many trials, and what trials can't tell us.

Why it matters: one trial is rarely the final word, and the trials you never hear about can change the whole picture.

Chapter 4 · p. 108 Exam Updated key study

What if we pooled every trial?

Meta-analysis

Collect every trial on a question (a systematic review) and combine the results with statistics. Many small trials become one big one: meta-analyses can include 100,000 patients or more.

The problems (Leonard)

Finding all the trials; judging their quality from what was published; and publication bias: trials with positive results are much more likely to be published.

Key study: Cipriani et al., Lancet, 2018

522 trials, 116,477 patients, 21 antidepressants: every one worked better than placebo for adults with major depression.

Amitriptyline
2.13
Reboxetine
1.37
Placebo
1.00

Odds ratio of improving, compared with placebo (1 = no better than placebo). 2.13 means the odds of responding were about twice as high as on placebo.

Why it matters: a meta-analysis is only as good as the trials that go in, which brings us to the trials that never come out.

Chapter 4 · p. 108 Exam Updated key study

Which trials never get published?

Guess: what share of antidepressant trials were positive in the published papers? In the FDA's own files?

74 trials of 12 antidepressants. Pick a view.

94% → 51%

positive in the journals → positive in the FDA's records

Turner et al., NEJM, 2008: 74 trials, 12 drugs, 12,564 patients

Of 36 trials the FDA judged negative or doubtful, 22 were never published and 11 were published as if positive.

Updated Since 2005, major journals only publish trials publicly registered before they start, so missing trials can be spotted.

Chapter 4 · pp. 108, 110 Updated

How many patients does a psychiatric trial need, and when can it stop?

50–60

patients in a typical placebo-controlled trial, lasting 6–8 weeks, though patients are usually treated for about 6 months

1,250–2,380

patients per group needed to show a 5% difference between two drugs (e.g. 60% vs 65% improving), because 20–30% of patients don't respond to either

Fixed or sequential?

Fixed-number trial: the size is set in advance. You can't "add patients until it's significant".

Sequential trial: planned checks along the way, stopping once a set result is reached (e.g. a 50% fall in the Hamilton score) or looks unlikely. Each extra look raises the risk of a false alarm, so the bar for "significant" is set higher.

Updated Intention to treat

Leonard notes trials often drop patients who stopped the drug. Today the main analysis counts everyone as randomised, so quitting because of side effects counts against the drug.

Why it matters: "no better than the old drug" may only mean the trial was too small and too short to tell.

Chapter 4 · pp. 109–111 Updated Lecture 3

Does newer mean better, and what does it cost?

The real cost

The drug is only about 10–15% of the total cost of treating depression, bipolar disorder or schizophrenia: tests, side effects, hospital or clinic care. Not treating costs too: early death, lost work, damaged social life.

Newer is better?

Leonard: quality-of-life studies show new antidepressants and antipsychotics (drugs for schizophrenia) beat older, cheaper ones.

Updated Two large trials, CATIE (USA, 2005) and CUtLASS (UK, 2006), found newer antipsychotics were not clearly better than older ones.

Prescribing guidelines rank drugs by the evidence behind them

Leonard's prescribing principles

Weigh risks and benefits with the patient · confirm the diagnosis · avoid polypharmacy (several drugs at once) · lowest effective dose, especially in older people · increase slowly · reduce slowly, at a rate set by the drug's half-life (Lecture 3), to avoid withdrawal-like symptoms.

Big ideas

Who doesn't know the treatment in a double-blind trial?
What does a Phase 1 study mainly test?
Three jobs of a placebo group?
A trial misses a drug that really works. Which error?
The biggest weakness of meta-analysis?

Take away: a good trial is randomised, blinded, placebo-controlled (ideally with a standard drug), big enough, and published whatever it finds. "Significant" means probably real, not necessarily important.
